teaser: Ten people, one shallow gold box, and some of the first convincing tears in painting.

lesson.text: Can a picture make you cry? Not a film with music, not a story with a hundred pages to grow attached to someone. One still image, on wood. Around 1435 a painter in Brussels named Rogier van der Weyden set out to do exactly that, and for the next two hundred years people said he had succeeded.

The moment is the evening of the Crucifixion. Christ is dead and his friends are lowering the body from the cross. There are ten figures, nearly life-size, on an oak panel about 2.2 meters high at its center and 2.6 wide (roughly 7 by 8.5 feet). You do not look at this group from a distance. You stand in it.

And where is the hill, the sky, the city of Jerusalem? Gone. Rogier shuts everyone inside a gold box barely deeper than a shelf. He is imitating the carved altarpieces of his day, wooden cases full of painted statues. Then he outdoes them: his statues have skin that bruises and eyes that have been crying.

The clients were not priests or princes. The panel was ordered by the crossbowmen's guild of Leuven, a kind of civic shooting club, for their chapel. Tiny crossbows dangle from the carved ornaments in the upper corners, the guild's badge.
With no landscape to wander into, your eye has only one place to go: faces and hands. Rogier gives each mourner a different way of grieving, the way people at a real funeral never cry alike.

lesson.title: Four ways to grieve
lesson.text: Move from the left edge to the right, then down.

spots.title: Hidden eyes
spots.text: The woman at the far left presses a white cloth into one eye. On the original, clear tears run down her cheek, each with its own tiny highlight.

spots.title: A man's tears
spots.text: The man in gold brocade who carries Christ's legs looks down, his mouth pulled tight, his eyes red and wet. He is trying to keep his composure and not managing.

spots.title: Twisted hands
spots.text: Mary Magdalene bends her whole body into a knot, fingers locked together and wrenched to one side. You cannot see her eyes. The hands say it.

spots.title: Beyond tears
spots.text: Mary, the mother, has fainted. Her face is as gray-white as her son's, her eyes barely open. Tears have stopped at the edge of her eyelids.

lesson.text: Those drops were a technical feat. A tear is a bead of water with a spark of light on it and skin showing through. Oil paint, slow-drying and transparent in thin layers, could do that. Older egg-based paint could not. Religious writers of the time urged believers to feel Christ's suffering in their own bodies, and Rogier now had the means to help them.
All this emotion could easily turn into chaos. It does not, because under the weeping there is a design as strict as a diagram.
Four lines hold ten people together.

lines.label: The son
lines.text: Christ's body sags in a long slanting curve from his head on the left down to his crossed feet on the right, one arm hanging straight toward the ground.

lines.label: The mother
lines.text: Lower down, Mary collapses along the same slant, one arm dropping in the same way. Her body repeats his.

lines.label: Left bracket
lines.text: Saint John, in red, bends in from the left to catch Mary. His back makes a curve that closes that side of the group.

lines.label: Right bracket
lines.text: Mary Magdalene's bowed figure curves the other way. The two outer figures work like a pair of parentheses, and nothing spills out.

lesson.text: Mary's body echoes her son's on purpose. The word compassion literally means “suffering with”, and Rogier paints it as a shape: two bodies falling in the same line.

The blue of Mary's robe is ultramarine, made by grinding lapis lazuli, a stone mined in the mountains of what is now Afghanistan. It was among the most expensive colors a painter could buy, and contracts often stated how much of it had to be used.

Between the two falling bodies, their hands almost meet: his pierced one, hers limp, a few centimeters apart. Below them lie a skull and a bone. The hill of the Crucifixion was called Golgotha, the place of the skull, and legend said the first man, Adam, was buried there. One person in the group, though, is already thinking about what comes next.
Someone has brought what is needed to prepare the body for burial. Can you find the object?

spots.title: The ointment jar
spots.text: The bald, bearded man at the back holds a tall white jar with a lid. It contains the perfumed ointment used to anoint the dead.

lesson.text: The jar stands right next to Mary Magdalene, and it is her sign. In the Gospels she is the one associated with precious ointment, so painters gave her a jar the way they gave Saint Peter his keys. Even in a scene this raw, Rogier keeps the old labels that told viewers who was who.

A century later Mary of Hungary, sister of Emperor Charles V, wanted the panel badly enough to trade the guild's chapel a church organ and a painted copy for it. Her nephew Philip II took it to Spain. An old account says the ship carrying it went down and the well-packed panel floated.

Rogier never signed it, or any other picture we know. It did not matter. Painters copied this group for generations, borrowing a hand here, a fainting pose there. It now hangs in the Prado in Madrid. As for the question at the start: stand in front of the man in gold brocade for a minute, and see how long you can stay dry-eyed.

quiz.question: Who ordered the painting?
quiz.explanation: The guild commissioned it for its chapel and tiny crossbows hang in the corners.

quiz.question: Why is there no landscape behind the figures?
options: Rogier imitates a shallow carved altarpiece full of painted statues
The background was cut off later
quiz.explanation: The gold box mimics carved wooden altarpieces and forces attention onto faces and hands.

quiz.question: What does the similar pose of Mary and Christ express?
options: That the painter reused a drawing to save time
quiz.explanation: Her collapsing body repeats the line of his to show she shares his suffering.

quiz.question: Why could Rogier paint such convincing tears?
options: He glued glass beads to the panel
Oil paint can be laid in thin transparent layers
quiz.explanation: Slow-drying, transparent oil paint could render a clear drop with a highlight.

quiz.question: What did Mary of Hungary give in exchange for the panel?
options: An organ and a painted copy
quiz.explanation: She traded the chapel a church organ and a copy of the painting.

facts.text: Rogier van der Weyden signed the painting on the foot of the cross.
facts.explanation: No signed painting by Rogier is known.

facts.text: The blue of Mary's robe comes from a stone mined in what is now Afghanistan.
facts.explanation: Ultramarine was made by grinding lapis lazuli.

facts.text: The figures are tiny, like those in a prayer book.
facts.explanation: They are nearly life-size, on a panel about 2.6 meters wide.
